title: Madagascar Healthshed Clinic Data Manual
text:
0.1 Accessing and using the data
The Madagascar Healthshed Clinic Data brings together monthly clinic-reported counts, facility metadata, diagnosis definitions, and healthshed geography for research on health and environmental exposures in Madagascar. Historical observations cover 2010–2024, with a separately ingested 2025–2026 extension.
Healthsheds represent catchment areas linking villages to a central clinic. The dataset provides a 2022 spatial reference for relating clinic reports to catchment geography and environmental exposures. A historical healthshed does not establish a clinic’s catchment for every year.
The cleaned database contains:
These are reported counts, not individual patient records or population prevalence estimates. Missing categories can reflect unavailable or unreported information and must not automatically be converted to zero. Definitions and reporting coverage change across collection eras; the reader’s guide explains these boundaries and presents measured historical comparisons and the observed extension.
Start with Access the data with Stagecoach, then read A Reader’s Guide to the Cleaned Database for file layouts, joins, missingness, and analysis examples. The dataset is not yet in the Depot; Stagecoach currently symlinks the shared release directory into your analysis project. Choose one complete, versioned release for an analysis.

title: Madagascar Healthshed Clinic Data Manual
text:
0.2 Operating the pipeline
Pipeline operators should continue with the three operator groups:

Setup: operator overview, rendering, project contracts, governance, and the historical pipeline map.
Infrastructure: environment setup, container construction, R dependencies, and the runner.
Pipeline: input staging, cleaning, validation, release packaging, and reader-guide evidence generation.

The pipeline implements historical curation from the frozen May 2025 archive, a separate 2025–2026 extension, and versioned Parquet packaging with a Frictionless descriptor. The default release remains an internal candidate; full all-variable scientific equivalence and external publication remain separate review decisions.

title: 2  Access the Data With Stagecoach
text:
Use Stagecoach to symlink the shared releases into your own analysis project on FASRC. The dataset is not yet in the Depot. Its current release directory is:
/n/holylabs/cgolden_lab/Lab/frontier/works/prospectors/prospectorMDGHealthshedClinicData/data/outputs/releases
You can use a completed release without running the curation pipeline or building its container. The reader’s guide explains the files, joins, diagnosis definitions, and interpretation limits.






Important Prerequisite: Prepare Your Analysis Project



You need an authorized FASRC account with read access to the shared release directory and your own analysis project. A symlink uses your existing file permissions; it does not grant access. Keep the shared release read-only in your workflow and write analysis products in your own project.
Follow the Stagecoach installation and project setup instructions if needed. Run the following commands from your analysis project’s root.








Tip Procedure: Declare the Shared Releases in Stagecoach



If your analysis project does not already have a stagecoach_manifest.yml, create one:
stagecoach hail
Keep the generated Frontier, citizen, and project fields specific to your own analysis project. In its manifest, enable sources.01_gold_mine and add the following item to its items list. Merge this entry with any existing items. This is a manifest excerpt, not a replacement for the full manifest:
sources:
  01_gold_mine:
    enabled: true
    items:
      - name: mdg_healthshed_clinic_data
        path_regex: '/n/holylabs/cgolden_lab/Lab/frontier/works/prospectors/prospectorMDGHealthshedClinicData/data/outputs/releases'
        required: true
Stagecoach’s 01_gold_mine source supports FASRC symlinking from an explicit readable path. Here it points to the Prospector’s releases while the dataset awaits Depot availability. Set project.input_data_dir to your analysis project’s data/inputs directory to use the paths shown below.
Inspect the manifest, resolve any reported issues, and stage it:
stagecoach inspect --manifest stagecoach_manifest.yml
stagecoach stage --manifest stagecoach_manifest.yml
Stagecoach creates the directory symlink at <input_data_dir>/01_gold_mine/<item name>/<source basename>. With the configuration above, your project sees:
data/inputs/01_gold_mine/mdg_healthshed_clinic_data/releases








Tip Procedure: Choose One Complete Release



List the available versions through the staged link:
ls data/inputs/01_gold_mine/mdg_healthshed_clinic_data/releases/
Choose a complete v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<BUGFIX>/ directory containing datapackage.json and its listed resources. The initial declared version is v0.1.0; use it only once that package is complete and available. Directory existence alone does not establish completeness. The current package defaults to an internal candidate, so confirm that the chosen release is appropriate for your intended analysis.
Record the explicit version in analysis code, together with the manifest and release provenance. The symlink exposes the releases directory as it changes; selecting a named version keeps the analysis tied to that version. Use all tables from the same release. The reader’s guide lists the resources and shows how to load a diagnosis partition from this staged location.








Warning Check: Check the Link and Selected Package



For a completed v0.1.0 package, run the following checks from your analysis project. Substitute your selected version when needed:
test -L data/inputs/01_gold_mine/mdg_healthshed_clinic_data/releases
readlink -f data/inputs/01_gold_mine/mdg_healthshed_clinic_data/releases
test -r data/inputs/01_gold_mine/mdg_healthshed_clinic_data/releases/v0.1.0/datapackage.json
The resolved link should be the shared release directory printed above. Before loading data, check that every resource listed in the selected datapackage.json exists and matches its recorded checksum. Retain the descriptor, version, and provenance in your analysis record.

title: 3  A Reader’s Guide to the Cleaned Database
text:
3.1 Find the data you need
The database brings together monthly clinic reports from Madagascar, with historical observations from 2010–2024 and a separately ingested 2025–2026 extension. Its three main components are clinic metadata, a diagnosis dictionary, and diagnosis files. Healthshed polygons provide the spatial reference for geographic analyses. These are clinic-reported counts, not individual patient records, population prevalence estimates, or complete surveillance of every illness in a catchment.
This guide adapts the archived cleaned-database README to the current Parquet release. The pipeline map explains how the original cleaning stages were reproduced; the remaining Pipeline pages document their rules and audits.
Intermediate reference tables support curation and investigation. They are not required for ordinary analysis of a completed release. The current release uses Parquet throughout; the archive’s CSV, Feather, RDS, and shapefile names are historical references rather than additional files readers must locate.

title: 3  A Reader’s Guide to the Cleaned Database
text:
3.2 Clinic metadata and spatial information
clinic_ID links the two metadata tables to diagnosis records. In the spatial table, n_month, first_report, and last_report summarize retained reporting history. Region/district information, facility type (fs_type), public/private status (pub_priv), and functional status (f_or_nf) describe the available reference information. Associated origin fields retain where attributes came from; these are not a complete monthly history of facility upgrades or status.
ID_checked records historical identity review, principally relevant to the pre-2020 code reconciliation. It is not a guarantee that every clinic identity is correct. clinic_x and clinic_y contain selected longitude and latitude; gps_source, gps_source_raw, and coordinate_status describe their evidence and availability. Newly encountered facilities may have missing coordinates.
Join clinic_spatial_metadata.clinic_ID to healthsheds2022.fs_uid to attach healthsheds. The current spatial file contains geometry_wkt, crs_wkt, is_empty, and reference_year. It is ordinary Parquet containing WKT, not GeoParquet. For example, after reading the table as x:
geometry <- sf::st_as_sfc(x$geometry_wkt, crs = x$crs_wkt[[1]])
healthsheds <- sf::st_sf(fs_uid = x$fs_uid, geometry = geometry)
Healthsheds describe the villages assigned to clinics in the 2022 reference; they do not establish a facility’s catchment for every year. has_healthshed indicates a nonempty matched polygon. Private clinics, facilities outside the 2022 sectorization, and unmatched villages may lack geometry. The archive’s counts of exceptional clinics were a historical snapshot and should not be reused as current counts.
For spatial analyses, the archived recommendation was to consider clinics with a healthshed or a reviewed neighbor_to_merge. This remains an analysis choice, not a filter applied to the released diagnoses. If combining a clinic with its suggested neighbor, document the pair and sum each clinic once; do not duplicate the neighbor’s existing totals. Inspect missing geometry and healthshed_temporal_status before extending a spatial analysis into 2025–2026.
The reporting table uses year and month; diagnosis files use cAnnee and cPeriode. fname is a source-family identifier, not a diagnosis variable:



fname

Historical source selection can retain a report from another source family when the expected file has no report; fname records what was actually used. clinic_database_code retains the source identifier for a clinic-month. When several historical candidates cannot be resolved, the current pipeline keeps one reporting row, leaves that code missing, sets database_code_ambiguous, and preserves candidates in audits/reporting_code_candidates.parquet.
The extension also records source_report_present and source_covered. An absent clinic report and a month absent from the supplied source coverage are different situations. A calendar row with fname = 0 is not an observed zero for every disease.

title: 3  A Reader’s Guide to the Cleaned Database
text:
3.3 Diagnosis dictionary
Each var identifies a harmonized variable. description_en and description_fr describe it; filename locates its diagnosis partition. wave1_colname, wave2_colname, wave3A_colname, and wave3B_colname record the source expressions. waves_available and the Wave 3 descriptions help interpret coverage and construction. Consult the expressions as well as the short English label: a variable can have different components in different collection eras, or be unavailable in an entire wave.
The dictionary retains both broader harmonized categories and finer categories available in only some waves. Variables can overlap. Adding every diarrhea or pneumonia search result can double-count cases; referrals can also be a subset of other age/sex totals. V identifiers and file1–file40 partition names are identifiers, not a clinical taxonomy or a recommendation to combine adjacent columns.
For example, V121 is the dictionary’s diarrhea category for ages 1–4 and is constructed from different source components across waves. V135 is pneumonia for ages 1–4 and has no Wave 2 expression. Its missing 2015–2019 segment in the figures is an unavailable definition, not evidence of zero pneumonia.
crumbs: 3  A Reader's Guide to the Cleaned Database

title: 3  A Reader’s Guide to the Cleaned Database
text:
3.4 Diagnosis files and interpretation
Each diagnosis partition contains clinic_ID, cAnnee, cPeriode, fname, and its assigned V columns. Retained partitions share a common clinic-month key set; wrong-source alternatives remain curation evidence rather than extra observations to append to the released diagnoses. Cleaning reconciles clinic identifiers, reduces repeated reports, chooses source families, and applies the dictionary’s wave-specific expressions.
Keep these distinctions when analyzing the measurements:

Entered zero: an observed count of zero.
Missing value: unavailable or unreported information; do not replace all missing values with zero. All-missing sums in the new extension remain missing.
Historical -1: a blank/sentinel in older data. Its handling depends on the variable construction; it is not a negative disease count.
Other negative sentinels, including -99: retained cleaning/ambiguity evidence requiring investigation before analysis.

Historical clinic IDs attempt to follow facilities through GESIS code changes and the switch to DHIS2 UIDs. Large name changes, reused codes, and incomplete review can still affect linkage. New-source identity decisions and candidate predecessors are retained in the release’s audits.
Collection transitions occurred around April 2015, January 2020, and January 2021. The additional 2025 deliveries introduce another source boundary and mid-2025 renaming changes. A jump in counts can reflect definitions, reporting coverage, source formatting, or epidemiology; the graph alone cannot identify the cause. The archive specifically cautioned about trauma, pneumonia, measles/meningitis notification categories, and malnutrition definitions. Its interpretation of tetanus trends is a historical hypothesis rather than a conclusion established by this migration. Birth variables refer to births recorded within clinics, and trauma categories refer to physical trauma, as described in the archived README; consult individual definitions before use.

section: 3.5 Historical comparison and the continuing series
text:
3.5 Historical comparison and the continuing series
The reference is the most recent archived data within the hand-delivered May 2025 ZIP, specifically data/clean/by_diagnosis_2024/file2.feather, rather than a later Drive copy. The archive and dictionary are checked against the reviewed baseline. The three examples are the dictionary variables V114 (simple malaria), V121 (diarrhea), and V135 (pneumonia), each for ages 1–4. They are individual variables, not sums of overlapping search results.
Their archived and current English labels and source descriptions match. V121 has different internal Wave 3B X identifiers in the two dictionaries; the comparison preserves this fact rather than assuming equal V labels alone establish semantic equivalence. Full dictionary and all-variable measurement equivalence remain separate investigations.






Figure 3.1: Monthly national totals in the frozen archive and current pipeline through 2024. Dashed blue and solid orange lines allow overlapping series to remain visible.



The totals sum nonnegative values across retained clinics in each source. Negative sentinel cells are excluded and all-missing months remain missing. There is no smoothing, interpolation of missing months, or conversion to population rates. Matching national totals would not by themselves establish agreement at individual clinics, so the diagnostic also aligns unique clinic_ID/year/month keys and compares the original cells, including missing values and sentinels. The evidence snapshot below reports that stricter check.
Measured snapshot, 10 November 2026: all three variables match exactly on all 550,845 shared historical clinic-months. This is 1,652,535 equal cells and zero unequal cells, treating paired missing values as equal and preserving sentinel distinctions. The selected fname also agrees at every shared key.



Historical coverage through 2024
Clinic-months




Present in both sources
550,845


Present only in the archive
39


Present only in the current pipeline
90



The unmatched rows remain explicit coverage differences; their causes have not been established by this diagnostic. Consequently, this is strong measured agreement for the three examples on shared observations, not complete archive equivalence. The monthly plots include each source’s own retained population rather than silently discarding unmatched rows.






Figure 3.2: The current pipeline’s observed diagnosis series, including the available 2025–2026 extension. Orange marks the new-delivery boundary; grey marks historical collection transitions.



The observed extension ends in July 2026 in this snapshot. The continuation contains newly ingested observations, not an extrapolation of the archive. It retains the same dictionary interface while the ingestion handles new headers, repeated deliveries, identity decisions, and missingness. The source-seam audits compare December 2024/January 2025 and May/June 2025 against corresponding earlier-year transitions. Their flags identify questions for review, not proof that a trend is epidemiological or permission to change a diagnosis mapping.






Figure 3.3: Number of clinics contributing nonnegative measurements to each plotted series. This is measurement availability for the selected variable, not the total national facility population.



Interpret the counts together with this coverage figure. A clinic with an entered zero contributes to coverage; a missing or negative cell does not. Changes in contributing facilities can alter totals without the same change in within-clinic disease burden. The extension may also end in an incomplete calendar year; compare equivalent months before comparing annual totals.
In these examples, measurement coverage drops at the start of the 2025 deliveries, particularly for malaria and pneumonia. The post-2024 series is a continuation of the data product, but it is not evidence of seamless reporting coverage. Treat an apparent level change across that boundary as a question to investigate, rather than interpreting it directly as a change in illness.






Tip Procedure: Load a Diagnosis of Interest From a Release



Search the dictionary, inspect the definitions, and deliberately choose the variables required for the analysis. This example selects one pneumonia variable and reads only its key fields and measurement from 2020 onward:
# Run from your analysis project after staging with Stagecoach.
# Replace v0.1.0 with the complete version selected for your analysis.
release <- "data/inputs/01_gold_mine/mdg_healthshed_clinic_data/releases/v0.1.0"
package <- frictionless::read_package(file.path(release, "datapackage.json"))
dictionary <- duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb(
  file.path(release, "diagnosis_dictionary.parquet"), prudence = "stingy"
) |> dplyr::collect()

hits <- dictionary |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("pneumonia", description_en, ignore.case = TRUE))
hits |> dplyr::select(var, description_en, waves_available, filename)

wanted <- hits |> dplyr::filter(var == "V135")
stopifnot(nrow(wanted) == 1L)
pneumonia <- duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb(
  file.path(release, "by_diagnosis", paste0(wanted$filename, ".parquet")),
  prudence = "stingy"
) |>
  dplyr::filter(cAnnee >= 2020L) |>
  dplyr::select(clinic_ID, cAnnee, cPeriode, fname, dplyr::all_of(wanted$var)) |>
  dplyr::collect()
Keep year/month filters and column selection before collect() to limit memory use. To attach reporting metadata, match clinic_ID, cAnnee = year, and cPeriode = month; attach spatial attributes by clinic_ID. Check join cardinality before interpreting totals. Frictionless inventories the package; DuckDB reads the Parquet and sf reconstructs WKT geometry.








Warning Check: Check the Scope of an Agreement Claim



Three example series can demonstrate agreement or identify discrepancies in those series. They cannot certify all variables, every identity link, or the scientific interpretation of a temporal change. Complete schema/key validation, byte-identical release-copy checks, selected-cell comparisons, and full scientific equivalence answer different questions.
Before analysis, confirm the selected release version, inspect variable definitions, check join cardinality, and account for reporting coverage and missingness. Record those choices with the analysis. Operators can use Evidence maintenance to reproduce and test the comparison snapshot.

title: 4  Pipeline Operator Overview
text:
4.1 Operator workflow
This section is for maintainers who build the computational environment, curate the source data, validate outputs, or package a new release. For analysis of an existing release, start with Access the data with Stagecoach and the reader’s guide.
The Quarto Manual is the source of truth for pipeline configuration and command-line tools. It separates three operations:
No render is permitted to inspect or transform protected source data. The reader’s guide embeds explicitly generated national aggregate figures; protected source records and clinic-level evidence remain in the governed workspace. Evidence maintenance documents how operators rebuild those figures and verify their scope.
Work through Setup, Infrastructure, and Pipeline, in that order. Setup establishes the repository contract, rendering boundary, governance, and migration baseline. Infrastructure constructs the runtime. Pipeline pages declare source staging, transformations, checks, and release packaging. Stagecoach owns input staging; tracked notebook parameters own transformation and release choices.

title: 4  Pipeline Operator Overview
text:
4.2 Prior Work & Plan
This project has been ongoing for several years, with several hands having been involved in data management. Contact persons worth keeping in mind:

Chris Golden (PI, present)
G. DeNicola (Post Doc, present)
Marissa Childs (Post Doc, 2024(?))
Tinashe M. Tapera (RSE, present)


Human decision required: confirm the project participants, their roles, and the accountable data steward before source data is staged or inspected.

In general, there are 2 major “blocks” of data: pre-DHIS2, and post.
Pre-implementation of DHSI2, the data were processed ad-hoc and within their means, and post, the introduction of DHIS2 standards made manual fixes and adjustments far less prevalent. In our reproduction of the pipeline, we expect the same truth to hold in implementation. We will keep obvious manual fixes and patches as they are in the pre-DHIS2 data, as there is little we can do to confidently improve on spaghetti code without a comparable true expected outcome to test against. Post DHIS2, we will improve code where necessary to communicate more clearly, or speed up a laborious task.

title: 4  Pipeline Operator Overview
text:
4.3 How To Read This Manual
Operator pages combine explanations, procedures, and checks.
Each workflow page follows the Quarto Manuals page contract: one prerequisite block establishes the starting state, one or more procedure blocks perform the work, and one check block verifies the outcome. Target declarations, file writes, and execution commands belong in procedures. Checks inspect the resulting targets or artifacts through assertions, summaries, plots, or test commands. Read the prose before each code chunk for its inputs, action, and expected result.
Long transformations are divided into named stages so the operator can inspect their handoffs. Dependencies between pages live in targets and tracked files. The public authoring render executes no protected-data analysis; diagnostic chunks are for an authorized data session, and synthetic tests can run without the staged sources.
After editing a page, check the block structure without executing its code:
python3 tests/check-manual-structure.py

# Madagascar Healthshed Clinic Data

Monthly clinic-reported counts from Madagascar are distributed with facility
metadata, a diagnosis dictionary, and healthshed geography. Historical
observations cover 2010–2024, with a separately ingested 2025–2026 extension.
These are reported counts; missing measurements are not automatically zeros.

## Accessing and using the data

Follow [Access the data with Stagecoach](notebooks/00_access-data.qmd), then the
[reader's guide](notebooks/00_data-guide.qmd) for file layouts, joins,
missingness, and analysis examples. The dataset is not yet in the Depot.
Use [Stagecoach](https://goldenplanetaryhealthlab.github.io/stagecoach/) to
symlink the shared release directory into your own analysis project:

```text
/n/holylabs/cgolden_lab/Lab/frontier/works/prospectors/prospectorMDGHealthshedClinicData/data/outputs/releases
```

Choose one complete version and retain its `datapackage.json` and provenance
with your analysis. The default package remains an internal candidate;
packaging does not constitute publication.

## Operating the pipeline

The Manual separates operator guidance into Setup, Infrastructure, and
Pipeline. Start with the [operator overview](notebooks/00_cover.qmd).
The Manual owns generated configuration and command-line entry points;
scientific execution occurs explicitly through a Singularity container and
a targets graph. Historical curation, the separate 2025–2026 extension,
validation, and immutable Parquet packaging with a Frictionless descriptor
are implemented. Full archived measurement equivalence and publication
remain separate review decisions.

Only the reviewed national aggregate figures and their comparison summaries
are included in the Manual; protected source records and clinic-level
evidence remain outside the rendered Manual and version control.

## Render the Manual

```sh
scripts/render-isolated --profile authoring
scripts/render-isolated --profile emit
```

The authoring profile updates the rendered Manual. The emit profile also
synchronizes generated scripts and configuration from reviewed `.qmd` source.

## Build and operate the environment

Follow the rendered Infrastructure pages in `docs/infrastructure/`. After the
runtime image and frozen R library exist:

```sh
scripts/mdg-healthshed-clinic-data
scripts/mdg-healthshed-clinic-data exec uvr run scripts/run-pipeline.R
```

With no subcommand, the container runner opens a shell in the repository.
Commands require the explicit `exec` subcommand.

title: 5  Render In Isolation
text:
Use scripts/render-isolated from the repository root. It renders a private, data-free staging copy so concurrent jobs do not share Quarto’s mutable cache. Only a successful site and files recorded by quarto-emit are promoted back.






Important Prerequisite: Confirm The Render Boundary



The host needs bash, rsync, mktemp, python3, and quarto. Do not run two publishing renders against the same checkout simultaneously because both would promote to the same docs/ directory.








Tip Procedure: Emit The Isolated Render Wrapper



#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

script_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
project_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "${script_dir}/.." && pwd)
stage_dir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/quarto-render.XXXXXXXX")
trap 'rm -rf -- "$stage_dir"' EXIT

export XDG_CACHE_HOME="${stage_dir}/xdg-cache"
export XDG_DATA_HOME="${stage_dir}/xdg-data"
export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="${stage_dir}/xdg-runtime"
mkdir -p "$XDG_CACHE_HOME" "$XDG_DATA_HOME" "$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR"

# The Manual does not consume protected data or mutable runtime state.
rsync -a \
  --exclude '.git' \
  --exclude '.jj' \
  --exclude '.quarto' \
  --exclude '.spack-env' \
  --exclude '.uvr' \
  --exclude '_targets' \
  --exclude 'artifacts' \
  --exclude 'data' \
  --exclude 'docs' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/.quarto' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/_site' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/site_libs' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/*labbook' \
  "$project_dir/" "$stage_dir/project/"

(
  cd "$stage_dir/project"
  quarto render notebooks "$@"
)

emit_manifest="$stage_dir/project/.quarto/quarto-emit-manifest.tsv"
stage_project=$(realpath -e "$stage_dir/project")
if [[ -f "$emit_manifest" ]]; then
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r emitted_path source_page; do
    [[ -n "$emitted_path" && -n "$source_page" ]] || continue
    case "$source_page" in
      "$stage_project"/notebooks/*) ;;
      *) echo "Refusing emit source outside notebooks: $source_page" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    staged_file=$(realpath -e "$(dirname "$source_page")/$emitted_path") || {
      echo "Generated file is missing: $emitted_path" >&2
      exit 1
    }
    case "$staged_file" in
      "$stage_project"/*) ;;
      *) echo "Refusing emit target outside staged project: $staged_file" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    destination="$project_dir/${staged_file#"$stage_project"/}"
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$destination")"
    # Promote provenance together with code: temporary paths must not change
    # generated file hashes or point reviewers to a deleted staging tree.
    python3 - "$staged_file" "$stage_project" "$project_dir" <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import sys

emitted = Path(sys.argv[1])
staging = sys.argv[2].encode() + b"/"
repository = sys.argv[3].encode() + b"/"
lines = emitted.read_bytes().splitlines(keepends=True)
prefixes = (b"# Source: ", b"-- Source: ", b"<!-- Source: ", b"/* Source: ")
for index in range(min(4, len(lines))):
    if lines[index].startswith(prefixes):
        lines[index] = lines[index].replace(staging, repository, 1)
emitted.write_bytes(b"".join(lines))
PY
    rsync -a "$staged_file" "$destination"
  done < "$emit_manifest"
fi

rsync -a --delete "$stage_dir/project/docs/" "$project_dir/docs/"








Tip Procedure: Render The Manual Or Emit Project Files



Use the default profile for documentation and the explicit profile for file generation:
scripts/render-isolated --profile authoring
scripts/render-isolated --profile emit








Warning Check: Verify The Wrapper



Source headers are rebased only when generated files are promoted, so each render retains the repository source path rather than the temporary staging directory. Code bodies and embedded data paths are left byte-for-byte intact.
Confirm shell syntax and the presence of the rendered index after the authoring procedure completes.
bash -n scripts/render-isolated
python3 tests/check-render-source-provenance.py
test -s docs/index.html

title: 6  Project Contract
text:
The pipeline uses data/inputs, data/intermediates, and data/processed:

data/inputs is the immutable staged-input boundary;
data/intermediates contains derived Parquet files tracked as file targets;
data/processed contains candidate and versioned release artifacts;
notebooks owns the Manual and pipeline declarations;
scripts contains generated command-line entry points;
containers contains generated recipes and local runtime configuration;
artifacts/containers contains unversioned SIF images;
_targets contains unversioned targets state.

For the existing-wave migration, the hand-delivered May 2025 ZIP is the sole source of scientific inputs and comparison data. The periodically synced Google Drive/rclone tree is excluded from that migration because it can drift. The separate 2025–2026 deliveries are not in this ZIP: pages 26–28 survey their explicitly supplied source roots and plan a separately approved frozen input manifest. Their survey scaffolding is not registered in the production graph and does not change the historical comparison baseline. Page 16 extracts selected, unmodified source members under data/intermediates/archive_sources/; these source copies retain their original formats and are tracked as files. All other persisted transformation products remain Parquet.
Workflow data stays in ordinary targets objects or in Parquet files tracked with format = "file". Source files retain their original formats and are also tracked as file targets. The pipeline map records the convention and its application across the notebooks.

The legacy source is sandbox/madagascar_clinic_data_cleaning/scripts/. This page maps all 11 files in that directory to the pipeline notebooks that carry, or would carry, their responsibilities. The summaries below come from reading those files and the current notebooks; the legacy scripts were not executed to prepare this map. Counts recorded in legacy comments are historical observations, not newly verified results.
Source links use GitHub line anchors pinned to the local legacy checkout’s commit 31e0769683e133e136b09ac0c6608c5a12657a9a. The line ranges and file contents were checked locally against that commit; the GitHub URLs were not accessed. Pinning the revision keeps these references stable if the upstream branch changes. References to commented code are identified as such in the descriptions.
Artifact paths in the script summaries retain the legacy layout and spelling so that missing or inconsistent handoffs remain visible. They describe the old workflow; replacement storage locations still follow the new project’s staging and release contracts.
Existing, in development means a replacement notebook contains relevant code, not that migration or equivalence testing is complete. Planned means the page records a detailed migration contract, proposed target boundaries, and acceptance checks, but does not implement or wire those targets. Proposed remains available for destinations not yet created. A plan page does not establish scientific equivalence or a successful build.
Each implementation notebook should explain the scientific operation before its code: what one row represents, which input supplies each decision, what changes between stages, and what evidence would establish that the result is correct. A notebook can contain several targets while retaining one coherent responsibility.

text:
8.2 Workflow data storage convention
Across our workflows, keep all data in targets objects or in Parquet files tracked as file targets. In-memory tables, lists, and spatial sf objects remain ordinary targets. When a transformation persists data outside the target store, it writes Parquet and returns the path from a target declared with format = "file". A path stored in an ordinary character target does not itself track the file’s contents. A _parquet suffix documents the format; it does not replace the file-target declaration.
Branch-driver path vectors are ordinary targets containing selection metadata. When processing files individually, map that vector into a format = "file" target with its own pattern, then map the transformation over those file branches. A static file target treats its returned paths as one indivisible bundle, so it cannot be used as the dimension for per-file branching.
Staged source files retain their original CSV, Excel, ZIP, or spatial formats and provenance, and are also tracked as file targets. Temporary extraction and scratch files can exist within a target’s execution; downstream stages consume the returned object or tracked Parquet artifact. Diagnostic notebook queries use tar_read() or tar_load() and do not create separate persistent data copies. Ordinary targets may use RDS internally in the target store; the convention concerns how workflow data is handed between stages.
In tangled notebooks, #| format: file applies to every assignment in that code chunk. Keep path declarations in separate chunks from in-memory data transformations so tables are not accidentally declared as file paths.
The legacy filenames below remain historical evidence. Replacement handoffs follow this convention, including recommendations for notebooks still to be implemented.

8.3.7 Reproduce the archive inspection
This read-only command inventories members without extracting the repository or running R. It prints active and commented writer sites separately for review, expands the diagnosis families, lists embedded reference members, and recomputes the selected byte hashes. The top-level inventory has 960 regular files after excluding .DS_Store and entries outside the repository root (including AppleDouble __MACOSX/ entries); this count includes .git/. Its SHA-256 fingerprint over sorted relative_path<TAB>size<TAB>CRC32 records joined by newlines, with no trailing newline, is f00e476d2e904a29684e97f4fbe1aab7cd85492221b126cc10c8eef713c6ea84. This fingerprints the directory metadata, not the entire ZIP byte stream.
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath
from io import BytesIO
import hashlib
import re
import zipfile

archive = Path("data/inputs/01_gold_mine/gdn_datafreeze_may2025/"
               "madagascar_clinic_data_cleaning.zip")
root = "madagascar_clinic_data_cleaning/"
with zipfile.ZipFile(archive) as z:
    members = {
        i.filename.removeprefix(root): i for i in z.infolist()
        if i.filename.startswith(root) and not i.is_dir()
        and PurePosixPath(i.filename).name != ".DS_Store"
    }
    records = "\n".join(
        f"{name}\t{i.file_size}\t{i.CRC:08x}"
        for name, i in sorted(members.items())
    )
    print("Archive bytes:", archive.stat().st_size)
    print("Inventory files / SHA-256:", len(members),
          hashlib.sha256(records.encode()).hexdigest())
    writers = re.compile(r"write\.csv|write_feather|saveRDS|st_write|"
                         r"tmap_save|ggexport|ggsave|R CMD BATCH")
    for name, i in sorted(members.items()):
        if name.startswith("scripts/") and name.endswith((".R", ".slurm")):
            content = z.read(i)
            print("SCRIPT", name, "SHA-256", hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest())
            for n, line in enumerate(content.decode("utf-8-sig").splitlines(), 1):
                if writers.search(line):
                    state = "commented" if line.lstrip().startswith("#") else "active"
                    print(n, state, line.strip())
    for name, i in sorted(members.items()):
        if name.startswith(("data/clean/", "data/intermediate/", "scratch/")) or (
            "wave3_with_keys" in name or "/oreillon_" in name
        ):
            print("MEMBER", name, i.file_size, f"{i.CRC:08x}")
    with zipfile.ZipFile(BytesIO(z.read(root + "data/intermediate_ref_tables.zip"))) as nested:
        for i in nested.infolist():
            if not i.is_dir() and "__MACOSX/" not in i.filename and not i.filename.endswith(".DS_Store"):
                print("EMBEDDED", i.filename, i.file_size, f"{i.CRC:08x}")
    for name in (
        "scratch/dictionary_test2.csv", "data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv",
        "data/intermediate/w2010_2019_clinicID.rds", "data/clean/w2010_2019_clinicID.rds",
        "data/intermediate/clinic_reporting_track.feather",
        "data/clean/by_diagnosis_2024/clinic_reporting_track.feather",
    ):
        print("BYTES SHA-256", name, hashlib.sha256(z.read(root + name)).hexdigest())

text:
8.6 How the responsibilities connect
Three different kinds of mapping are involved. The facility mapping links a year-specific GESIS code to a DHIS2 facility UID. The clinic identity crosswalk follows a clinic through code and name changes. The diagnosis dictionary defines comparable measurement variables across reporting systems. The first two identify who reported; the third defines what was reported.
The spatial branch assigns administrative areas called fokontany (FKT) to clinics and unions their polygons into healthsheds. These are based on the 2022 sectorization. Their use alongside earlier reporting data does not itself establish historical catchment boundaries.
The diagram shows the intended scientific handoffs, including planned notebooks. It is a responsibility map, not a claim that all these dependencies are already implemented in _targets.R.











The Wave 3 preparation script also reads the original facility mapping to attach descriptive columns. It does not read the cleaned mapping produced by script 1. That separate use is described below because it affects join cardinality and should remain visible during migration.

text:
8.7 0 — Prepare the Wave 3 source table
Source: 0_prep_w3_kevin_translated.R. Destination: 18_page-prep-w3.qmd.
This script translates the earlier Wave 3 preparation into R. It recursively reads the RMA CSV exports, adjusts inferred logical columns to numeric so that sparsely populated measurements can be read, drops two organisation-unit description/code fields, and combines the tables. It then groups by organisationunitid and periodname, taking the maximum of each remaining field and replacing numeric negative infinity from all-missing groups with missing values. This is a maximum rule, not an addition of reports. See CSV type handling, lines 25–38; file discovery, column removal, and combination, lines 43–81; maximum reduction, lines 161–168.
Next, it reads the original DHIS2–GESIS mapping, selects facility UID, GESIS code, type, and name, removes exact duplicates and missing UIDs, and joins those attributes to the Wave 3 data by UID alone. It adds the legacy V1 row index. Finally, for periods after 202300, it substitutes three renamed breastfeeding and mosquito-net fields into their earlier column names and drops the replacement columns. See crosswalk preparation, lines 191–212; UID join and row index, lines 233–243; period-specific substitutions, lines 264–272.
Handoff: the script writes data/raw/from_Kevin/wave3_with_keys_may2_v3.csv. Scripts 3 and 4A instead read wave3_with_keys.csv. The prepared table supplies both measurements and the column names/order used by the diagnosis dictionary. See script 0 output, lines 274–275; script 3 input and column numbering, lines 31–48; script 4A input, line 249.
Context for notebook 18: explain the two reductions now used to avoid holding all source tables in R: maximum within each file, then maximum across the file summaries. Explain all-missing behavior separately from zero values. The UID-only descriptive join can repeat a row when a UID has several mapping records; grouping the mapping by UID in the legacy script did not make it unique. Record the expected cardinality rather than assuming one UID implies one output row. The script’s opening comment limits scope to 2020–2022, but its reader is recursive and its final substitutions explicitly address 2023; the actual supported input period needs an explicit contract. See stated scope, lines 1–6; recursive reader, lines 51–53; 2023 substitutions, lines 264–272.
The replacement notebook already contains the per-file DuckDB reader and reducer, cross-file reduction, descriptive join, and substitutions. Its stopping-point prose and crosswalk input variable names are not yet consistent with all of that code. Treat it as a migration in progress.

8.8 1 — Clean the DHIS2–GESIS facility mapping
Source: 1_clean_mapping_dhis2_gesis.R. Destination: 19_page-clean-mapping-dhis2-gesis.qmd.
This script prepares the bridge between historical GESIS facility codes and DHIS2 UIDs. It reads the original mapping and gives the four UID columns explicit region, district, commune, and facility names. See source mapping and exclusions, lines 11–18; code checks, corrections, and known UID fill, lines 25–58.
The remaining work applies the reviewed workbooks and CSVs: fill other missing UIDs; interpret annotations for UID-years associated with multiple GESIS codes as keep, rename, or delete decisions; add reviewed codes absent from the original mapping; and apply individual corrections discovered while comparing the mapping with diagnosis data. Deletions use the relevant year, code, and UID so that an unrelated record sharing a code is not removed accidentally. See additional UID fills, lines 64–71; annotation interpretation, lines 83–89; keyed deletions and renames, lines 143–163; missing-code additions, lines 175–196; individual corrections, lines 201–231.

A GESIS code may legitimately map to different UIDs over time, and a UID-year may retain multiple GESIS codes; a global one-to-one assertion would change the legacy interpretation. The notebook already separates the eight legacy stages and retains multiplicity and name checks. Those checks document exceptions to interpret, not a reason to merge or discard records automatically. See legacy multiplicity and name diagnostics, lines 235–274.

text:
8.9 2 — Construct longitudinal clinic identities for Waves 1–2
Source: 2_wave1-2_construct_clinicID.R. Destination: 20_page-construct-clinic-ids.qmd.
The script starts from an inventory of distinct clinic records in each monthly file. The six identifying fields are clinic name, year, month, commune code, facility code, and source-file number (fname). Its active code reads an already saved inventory; the code that originally built that inventory is commented out. See commented inventory construction and active read, lines 22–37.
It corrects facility codes using the reviewed workbook and joins the cleaned mapping by corrected code and mapping year. In 2015, January–March use old GESIS codes and later months use new codes, except that records from fname == 1 retain the old codes. Three explicit exceptions prevent known incorrect UID assignments. Within a corrected-code/name pair, it fills an unambiguous UID, then fills missing type and mapped name from the group’s mode. The mode helper resolves ties by first occurrence, so input order matters. See code corrections, lines 42–50; 2015 mapping and three exceptions, lines 63–79; UID and attribute propagation, lines 98–125; mode tie behavior, lines 7–15.
The initial clinic_ID is the UID when available, otherwise corrected GESIS code plus cleaned clinic name. The script marks reviewed deletions with a missing ID, reconciles identities using verified shortened GESIS codes (“snips”), and then uses commune/name groups to reconcile remaining identities. Four ambiguous snips and the 2014 110543027 exception remain excluded from the relevant reconciliation rules. See provisional identity, lines 143–156; reviewed deletions, lines 158–169; verified snips and exclusions, lines 177–205; commune/name reconciliation and exception, lines 209–221.
Handoff: data/intermediate/w2010_2019_clinicID.rds and .csv, retaining original matching fields, corrected code, mapped type, and ID_checked. That flag records whether any mapped type in the identity group contains CSB; it is not a general certification that the identity is correct. Scripts 4A, 6, and 7 consume this crosswalk. See ID_checked definition and crosswalk outputs, lines 223–233.
Context for notebook 20: distinguish source inventory, code correction, year-aware UID assignment, UID propagation, provisional identity, reviewed deletion, and the two reconciliation steps. The current notebook rebuilds the inventory from the staged ZIP in DuckDB, decoding Windows-1252 before reduction and preserving file/row order. Corrections, mapping, and reconciliation now form one sequence of named data targets; the duplicate correction route has been removed. Compare identities and exception records with the legacy result, including missing IDs and mode ties.

8.10 3 — Construct the diagnosis dictionary across waves
Source: 3_construct_dictionary.R. Replacement: 21_page-construct-diagnosis-dictionary.qmd, existing and in development.
This script defines comparable variables across Wave 1, Wave 2, Wave 3A (2020), and Wave 3B (2021–2022). It combines the earlier-wave dictionary, reviewed cross-wave diagnosis mappings, actual Wave 3 column names, a separate 2020 anemia export, and supplementary diagnoses. It replaces the original Wave 1 diarrhea/pneumonia definitions and adds AVC and ULGEN entries that were absent from the main dictionary. See source dictionaries and replacement diagnoses, lines 31–66; AVC, ULGEN, and diarrhea/pneumonia additions, lines 69–92.
It interprets mapping notation such as alternatives, ranges, and sums; joins source descriptions to column identifiers; and aggregates source variables into common definitions. The within-Wave-3 mapping handles changed age bands and disease definitions, including anemia, severe acute malnutrition, and suspected versus confirmed diabetes. It retains earlier-wave variables without a Wave 3 match, excludes designated ignored categories, and assigns output variable names such as V1, V2, and so on. These V variables identify harmonized measurements; they have a different role from the Wave 3 source table’s V1 row index. See within-Wave-3 definition changes, lines 105–162; common-definition aggregation, lines 178–205; mapping notation and wave joins, lines 208–277; unmatched variables and V identifiers, lines 280–299.
The later stages enrich the dictionary with French and English descriptions, diagnostic-code descriptions, reporting-table descriptions, available waves, and output-file groups. They use existing translated material, live gtranslate calls, and manual wording corrections. The filename column partitions variables into 40 groups for diagnosis output. See existing translations and live diagnostic-code translations, lines 307–357; description assembly, wave availability, and output groups, lines 446–486; reporting-table translations and final wording corrections, lines 514–561.
Handoff: the active final write is scratch/dictionary_test2.csv, while script 4A expects data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv. The missing promotion or rename step is not established by this script. The dictionary’s per-wave expressions and filename assignments drive measurement cleaning. See dictionary scratch output, lines 580–581; script 4A dictionary input, lines 29–31.
Context for the replacement: explain source dictionaries and supplements, cross-wave equivalence rules, expression construction, and descriptive enrichment as separate stages. Wave 3 X1, X2, etc. are assigned from the prepared table’s column order, even though several joins now match on descriptions. Record that schema explicitly so a changed reader or column order cannot silently change a diagnosis. Preserve translation provenance rather than treating a fresh network translation as a fixed input. Checks should establish that referenced columns exist, summed terms are distinct, and each source-expression mapping is used as intended. See positional X identifiers, lines 31–48; mapping uniqueness and repeated-summand checks, lines 563–578.
The replacement notebook now records the prepared Parquet schema in s3_w3_column_dictionary_df, appending only missing anemia column names. It reduces replacement diarrhea/pneumonia inputs to unique definitions in DuckDB before collecting them. s3_diagnosis_dictionary_df is the small in-memory handoff, and s3_diagnosis_dictionary_parquet persists it as a file target. The graph declares these stages; it has not been executed as part of this migration.
Translations reuse the archived original description translations and the bilingual data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv member in the staged ZIP. s3_diagnosis_translation_provenance_df records those source members. Grouped diagnostic-code phrases are matched exactly after assembly; this replaces the legacy live translation calls without splitting phrases on punctuation. Conflicting lookup pairs fail, missing required code/table translations appear in s3_diagnosis_translation_gaps_df and stop the final handoff, and missing general English descriptions remain visible for review. 8.11 4A — Clean measurements and combine reporting waves
Source: 4A_clean_clinic_diagnosis.R. Destination: 22_page-clean-clinic-diagnosis.qmd, implemented and wired into targets; full-data parity remains a validation task.
This is the main measurement transformation. It consumes the clinic-ID crosswalk, diagnosis dictionary, monthly tall Waves 1–2 files, prepared Wave 3 data, and supplementary AVC, diarrhea/pneumonia, and anemia exports. The identity work determines which clinic a report belongs to; the dictionary determines how its measurements become comparable variables. See identity and dictionary dependencies, lines 29–51; earlier-wave source files and supplements, lines 108–128.
For Waves 1–2, it replaces the superseded Wave 1 diarrhea/pneumonia records, adds supplements, normalizes variable names, joins clinic IDs, and excludes the explicitly problematic UID qCHtCHkwqtQ. It drops clinic-month/file groups whose total reported value is not positive. Duplicate handling distinguishes identical repeats, differences caused only by missing values, and distinct values that the legacy rules sum. Unhandled conflicts receive the -99 sentinel. It then pivots measurements wide, adds expected but absent columns, and evaluates the dictionary separately for the two waves. See supplements, identity join, exclusions, and reporting filter, lines 121–154; duplicate classification and reductions, lines 160–196; wide conversion and dictionary evaluation, lines 198–236.
For Wave 3, it inserts the separate 2020 anemia data, assigns the positional X names expected by the dictionary, drops exact duplicate records, converts negative values in three designated variables to missing, and removes rows without positive measurements while excluding refrigerator-temperature fields from that reporting check. It applies Wave 3A expressions to 2020 and Wave 3B expressions to the later periods. See 2020 anemia insertion, lines 271–287; column numbering, deduplication, negatives, and reporting filter, lines 293–324; Wave 3A and 3B evaluation, lines 329–344.
Finally, it combines the waves and resolves overlapping reports using the expected source file for each period. It prefers that file when present; otherwise it keeps the closest available file number. The same selection logic supplies the reporting-history table. See reporting-history selection, lines 350–373; combined outputs and overlapping-file selection, lines 382–418.
Handoff: data/clean/by_diagnosis/<filename>.feather, separate <filename>_wrong_fname.feather files for discarded overlapping reports, and data/clean/by_diagnosis/clinic_reporting_track.feather. The tracking table records which file supplied each clinic-month, using zero for no retained report. Script 7 expects the tracker at data/intermediate/clinic_reporting_track.feather; the source scripts do not establish the intervening move or copy. See script 4A output directory, lines 22–25; tracker values and write, lines 350–373; retained and rejected diagnosis outputs, lines 404–418; script 7 tracker input, line 21.
Context for the replacement: document earlier-wave cleaning, Wave 3 cleaning, dictionary application, report selection, and output partitioning separately. The duplicate rules here differ from the maximum rule in script 0. Missing values, entered zeros, the temporary -1 missing-value sentinel, and the -99 conflict sentinel have different meanings. In sums, earlier-wave -1 values and Wave 3 missing values are replaced with zero; this does not justify replacing every missing measurement with zero. Preserve the excluded UID, negative-value rules, and fname tie behavior as explicit decisions to review during migration. See wave-specific missing values in sums, lines 53–72; temporary -1 sentinel, lines 198–200.

8.13 5 — Reconcile sectorization and construct 2022 healthsheds
Source: 5_clean_sect2022_construct_healthsheds.R. Implemented page: 23_page-construct-healthsheds.qmd, ordered targets with synthetic rule and graph checks.
This script connects the 2022 sectorization’s FKT assignments to administrative polygons, then unions the assigned polygons for each clinic. Its inputs include the sectorization table, OCHA/BNGRC boundaries and code lookup, reviewed matching files, manual geolocation corrections, the 2018 sectorization, and the cleaned GESIS–DHIS2 mapping. See spatial sources and sectorization schema, lines 54–100; 2018 sectorization and cleaned facility mapping, lines 309–328.
It first repairs geometry and separates Nosy Mitsio from a mainland polygon. It reconciles duplicated FKT codes while preserving the reviewed population totals, validates original codes, and fills missing matches from several rounds of reviewed fuzzy and manual matching. It attaches polygons and uses their topological relationships to identify isolated assignments. Some isolated matches are removed while explicitly protected manual matches remain. See geometry repair and Nosy Mitsio split, lines 56–88; duplicate FKT and population rules, lines 102–121; reviewed matching rounds and geometry joins, lines 123–228; topology checks and isolated-match removal, lines 230–275.
Later passes recover assignments using the 2018 sectorization, apply further manual matches and unmatches, and assign some remaining polygons through a close commune-name match when that commune has one clinic and the assignment does not worsen contiguity. Subsequent reviewed corrections move FKT between clinics, resolve duplicates, and split coastal islands into separately assigned geometry. The script records matching provenance in match_type and rebuilds healthsheds after successive correction passes. See 2018 recovery, lines 304–404; manual matches and unmatches, lines 406–459; commune matches and contiguity guard, lines 481–565; reviewed reassignments and duplicates, lines 585–664; coastal-island splits, lines 666–720; final reassignments and aggregation, lines 722–786.
The sect_to_shed() helper unions assigned polygons by facility UID, calculates population from distinct FKT UID/population pairs, and records matched-area counts, connected components, and polygon parts. Reviewed shared assignments can produce overlapping healthsheds; this is not simply a non-overlapping partition of Madagascar. See population, geometry, components, and polygon parts, lines 10–44; reviewed shared assignments, lines 102–105.
Handoff: data/intermediate/sectorization2022_cleaned.feather, data/intermediate/sectorization2022_cleaned_shapefile, and data/clean/healthsheds2022 plus healthsheds2022.rds. It also writes review maps and unmatched-clinic tables under scratch/. Scripts 6 and 7 consume the cleaned sectorization and healthsheds. See review maps and unmatched-clinic export, lines 805–967; sectorization and healthshed outputs, lines 969–1000.
Context for the replacement: organize the narrative around source geometry, matching evidence, assignment corrections, catchment aggregation, and residual exceptions. Preserve the precedence of correction rounds, population counting, overlap policy, island splits, and the distinction between connected components and polygon parts. The legacy comments report residual non-contiguous healthsheds even after all polygons are assigned; complete coverage and contiguity are separate properties. A shapefile is a group of companion files, so artifact tracking must cover the complete dataset. See historical residual-contiguity and coverage observations, lines 788–803.

8.14 6 — Compare location sources and select clinic coordinates
Source: 6_locate_clinics.R. Planned page: 24_page-locate-clinics.qmd, detailed plan; targets not implemented.
This script assembles candidate coordinates from the cleaned sectorization, MDDSS, WHO and UNICEF master lists, and a separate GPS source, using the clinic-ID crosswalk to connect historical GESIS codes to UIDs. It cleans coordinate formats, applies specific UID and duplicate-record corrections, and uses closest-name matches where a GESIS code has multiple possible identity matches. It also identifies likely clinic FKT by name and reported distance within the sectorization. See source reads and sectorization coordinates, lines 50–103; MDDSS identity and closest-name joins, lines 105–136; WHO corrections and coordinates, lines 138–180; UNICEF and GPS candidates, lines 182–211; FKT name/distance selection, lines 228–256.
It converts candidates to spatial points and tests whether each lies inside the matched FKT or the clinic’s healthshed. The selection rule first prefers WHO, sectorization, UNICEF, then MDDSS points contained in the matched FKT; it also considers GPS points contained in the healthshed. It then considers other points contained in the healthshed in the listed source order. If no point qualifies, it falls back to the matched FKT centroid, then the healthshed centroid, and finally an explicit missing-location state. See point conversion, containment, and source comparison, lines 273–312; coordinate-source precedence and centroid fallbacks, lines 314–329.
Handoff: data/intermediate/clinic_LL.rds, retaining candidate coordinates, containment evidence, FKT geometry, and the selected-source label which_use. Labels ending in 2 indicate selection through the later healthshed-based test. Script 7 uses these labels to extract the final coordinates. See selected-source labels, lines 314–329; location artifact write, lines 331–334.
Context for the replacement: explain candidate ingestion, identity matching, spatial comparison, and selection separately. The introductory source list is not the final selection policy; the actual which_use conditions are the operative rule. Name similarity helps join candidate records but does not independently establish that a coordinate is correct. Keep source provenance and distinguish a reported facility point from an inferred centroid. Document the coordinate reference system and preserve explicit unresolved cases.

8.17 Exploratory checks — Recover questions and reproducible comparisons
Source: data_checks.R. Destinations: 17_page-inspect-source-data.qmd, checks in the notebooks owning each transformation, and the planned 30_page-validate-migration.qmd.
This is a collection of investigations rather than one ordered production stage. It compares files and column names between 2021–2022 exports, 2023 exports, and a later 2023 delivery; compares clinic/period coverage and values; and explores CSV type inference under different readers and sampling limits. Later sections compare old and rebuilt Wave 3 tables and ordered versus unordered diagnosis dictionaries, tracing differences in missing values, column types, names, and individual measurements back to source exports. Several investigations are repeated with different local file paths. See export and column inventories, lines 10–116; coverage and value comparisons, lines 119–266; reader and type-inference experiments, lines 268–338; Wave 3 comparisons and source tracing, lines 357–613; dictionary comparisons and repeated investigations, lines 653–902.
The final section also performs a data transformation: it splits a combined 2021–2022 mumps export into separate year files and writes a 2021 subset containing the male 2–11-month variable plus metadata. Those writes go into the legacy raw directory. They should be accounted for as derived artifacts with a source dependency in the replacement workflow, rather than remaining an undocumented prerequisite. See mumps source, year split, and exports, lines 912–935; male 2–11-month subset and export, lines 938–954.
Handoff: mostly printed comparisons and interactive inspection, plus the three mumps CSV outputs. There is no single reusable validation report or uniform pass/fail contract in this file.
Context for the replacements: put source schema and coverage questions in notebook 17, preserve focused invariants with the transformation they test, and use the proposed validation notebook to record comparisons between equivalent legacy and replacement artifacts. Identify the exact source versions, align records by scientific keys, and compare missingness as well as values. Account for legitimate schema/format changes separately from scientific differences. Turning every exploratory statement into an automated assertion would preserve unfinished investigations as assumptions.

8.18 Assignment-to-target inventory
This inventory maps the legacy assignments to named responsibilities in the replacement graph. It is a design index; no targets are created or rewired by these tables.
Identifiers use script::variable, for example 1::mapping. The script keys match the filenames in the crosswalk; 999 denotes the utilities and checks denotes data_checks.R. A repeated variable is qualified by its stage because an in-place reassignment can represent a different scientific operation. Function-local values are listed with their owning operation, and short setup/read/normalization steps may share one target. Columns created inside mutate(), summarise(), or := belong to the assigned table; the important column stages are named in the rows rather than proposed as individual targets. Commented-out alternatives are not active assignments; the commented inventory builder in script 2 is retained as provenance for its active inventory read.
Existing means the exact name is declared in the current pipeline notebooks or _targets.R; it does not establish that the target has completed. A row can map to an existing target that already groups several legacy operations. Where the new pipeline changes storage or avoids a large intermediate, the mapping identifies the owning transformation, not an identical R object. Recommended names describe results or responsibilities still to be introduced or separated from a coarse target. Names shared across scripts identify the same producer/consumer handoff, not duplicate proposed targets. Recommended suffixes describe the intended R value or replacement Parquet format; implementation and branching remain to be decided.
Helper definitions are grouped with their owning data responsibilities in the legacy inventory below. In the current notebooks, tar_tangle() also turns top-level function assignments into targets; those use the _fn suffix. Diagnostic and exploratory objects are identified explicitly. Their inclusion preserves the question being asked; it does not promote every scratch expression to a validated scientific rule. The input inventories and current file selectors remain the common staging boundary. Rows for legacy final writes are included even when the write call has no assigned return value. Their replacement handoffs reuse ordinary data targets or name tracked Parquet artifacts.

8.18.1 Target naming convention
Use script-stage_domain_contextual-name_[modification-in-pipeline]_R-data-type, with underscores between words. The modification is optional. For example, s0_clinic_RMA_W3_group_max_parquet is the script 0 clinic/RMA Wave 3 group maximum artifact, and s1_gesis_xwalk_clean_df is the script 1 cleaned GESIS crosswalk in R.
The stage identifies the producing legacy script, not the notebook number or the consuming script: s0 through s7, with s4a for measurement cleaning. Exploratory checks use schecks. Shared utility operations keep the stage of their owning transformation. Common staging inputs use s0_pipeline.







Suffix
Value represented




df
In-memory data frame or tibble


sf
Spatial data frame with geometry


chr
Character vector, such as path-selection metadata or ZIP member names; referenced data files are tracked separately by file targets


list
Collection of tables, evidence, or plots


matrix
Comparison matrix


fn
Function assigned at the top level and tracked by tar_tangle()


parquet
Derived data-file paths tracked with format = "file"


csv, xlsx, zip, yml
Original source or manifest paths tracked with format = "file"; source formats are preserved



A file suffix describes the artifact format; format = "file" still determines whether targets tracks file contents. Renaming a target changes its cache identity. Subsequent builds may recompute renamed targets, and branch files named with tar_name() will use the new names.

A shared, recorded column-name mapping that permits comparison after storage changes

The actual helper implementation and matching parameters

title: 9  Local Operator Environment

direnv is an optional operator convenience, not part of the scientific environment. The container image fixes the R ABI and system libraries; the project-local uvr library fixes R packages.






Important Prerequisite: Enable The Local Convenience Layer



Install direnv and enable its shell hook before activating the emitted project configuration.

PATH_add "$PROJECT_DIR/scripts"


The file deliberately does not set library or compiler paths. Those belong inside the container.

test "$PROJECT_DIR" = "$PWD"

The builder image contains Rocky Linux 9 and a pinned Spack release, but no project packages. It resolves and installs the final runtime independently of the cluster’s mutable Spack installation.

command -v quarto

Bootstrap: docker
From: spack/rockylinux9:1.2.0

title: 11  Declare the Native Runtime
text:
spack.yaml declares the native runtime. R 4.5.1 is retained from the existing environment. The scientific workflow remains command-line-driven.
The x86_64_v3 baseline avoids tying the image to the build node. The system libraries follow the ERA5 and Nepal Climate Health examples, with the spatial requirements traced to legacy stages 5–7 and their shared utility script.
The native layer includes both FlexiBLAS, which Spack’s R installation uses, and OpenBLAS. The latter is an explicit runtime requirement because binary R packages resolved by uvr can link directly to the libopenblas.so.0 SONAME instead of going through R’s FlexiBLAS interface. Declaring OpenBLAS as a root spec ensures that its shared libraries are linked into the final Spack view.
The geospatial layer is a coherent Spack build of GDAL, GEOS, PROJ, SQLite, and UDUNITS-2. sf needs GDAL/GEOS/PROJ; its R dependency units needs libudunits2.so.0. Declaring sf in uvr.toml installs R code but cannot provide these native libraries. In the previous image, ldd reported missing UDUNITS, GDAL, GEOS, and PROJ libraries, so changing the existing search path would not repair the runtime. The installed binary also requested libgdal.so.30; a newer GDAL can have a different ABI. Build R packages from source against this image, as described on page 14.







Native requirement
Evidence and purpose




gdal, geos, proj, sqlite

title: 12  Customize and Build the Runtime
text:
The Jinja extension adds uvr, Quarto, ARF, and the Spack view to Spack’s generated Singularity recipe. ARF is installed from its pinned, checksummed Linux Rust-binary release. The image supplies R and its native runtime dependencies; uvr retains ownership of project-library and cache resolution at runtime.
The extension configures only image-owned executable, header, metadata, and shared-library search paths. It does not set UVR_LIBRARY, UVR_CACHE_DIR, R_LIBS_USER, or R_LIBS: those paths are project state, so uvr resolves them after the repository is mounted at /work.
ARF dynamically loads R’s C API rather than merely starting an R subprocess. The template therefore preserves the environment emitted by Spack’s parent template, including the R library directory contributed by environment activation. The ARF smoke test starts a headless R session under --cleanenv- equivalent image conditions, which catches a missing libR.so or one of its transitive native libraries.
The container also owns a UTF-8 locale invariant: LANG and LC_ALL are set to C.UTF-8 in the image environment. The runner uses --cleanenv, which otherwise leaves R in the ASCII C locale. In that locale, R’s list.files() turns a valid combining-accent filename byte sequence into literal text such as <cc><81>, creating a path that cannot exist. Setting the invariant in the image makes filename enumeration deterministic and independent of the host login locale. The build-time %test runs before Singularity applies this image environment, so the post-build verification below is the check that the invariant is actually active at runtime.
Following the ERA5 and Nepal runtime templates, the spatial libraries are linked into the same immutable view as R. Keep Spack’s inherited environment: it carries data-file paths such as the UDUNITS XML database as well as native library paths. Image acceptance checks the native layer without a project R library. After rebuilding, page 14 installs R packages from source and exercises the complete geospatial runtime on synthetic data.






Important Prerequisite: Confirm The Builder And Container Runtime



command -v singularity
test -r artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif









Tip Procedure: Emit The Final-Image Extension



{% extends "container/singularity.def" %}

{% block build_stage %}
{{ super() }}
  set -euo pipefail
  UVR_VERSION=0.4.6
  QUARTO_VERSION=1.9.38
  ARF_VERSION=0.5.2
  ARF_ARCHIVE=arf-console-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.xz
  ARF_SHA256=64bb48569e79b91d0b258445173a78b5ad74e9274e8fd17b524c64531405b987
  curl --fail --location --show-error --output /tmp/uvr.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/nbafrank/uvr/releases/download/v${UVR_VERSION}/uvr-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz"
  mkdir -p /opt/uvr/bin
  tar -xzf /tmp/uvr.tar.gz -C /opt/uvr/bin
  rm -f /tmp/uvr.tar.gz
  /opt/uvr/bin/uvr --version | grep -Fx "uvr ${UVR_VERSION}"
  curl --fail --location --show-error --output /tmp/quarto.tar.gz \
    "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-amd64.tar.gz"
  mkdir -p /opt/quarto
  tar -xzf /tmp/quarto.tar.gz -C /opt/quarto --strip-components=1
  rm -f /tmp/quarto.tar.gz
  /opt/quarto/bin/quarto --version | grep -Fx "${QUARTO_VERSION}"
  curl --fail --location --show-error --output "/tmp/${ARF_ARCHIVE}" \
    "https://github.com/eitsupi/arf/releases/download/v${ARF_VERSION}/${ARF_ARCHIVE}"
  printf '%s  %s\n' "${ARF_SHA256}" "/tmp/${ARF_ARCHIVE}" | sha256sum --check --strict
  mkdir -p /tmp/arf /opt/arf/bin
  tar -xJf "/tmp/${ARF_ARCHIVE}" -C /tmp/arf
  install -m 0755 "/tmp/arf/${ARF_ARCHIVE%.tar.xz}/arf" /opt/arf/bin/arf
  /opt/arf/bin/arf --version | grep -Fx "arf ${ARF_VERSION}"
{% endblock %}

{% block final_stage %}
{{ super() }}
%files from build
  /opt/uvr /opt/uvr
  /opt/quarto /opt/quarto
  /opt/arf /opt/arf
  /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock
%post
  set -eu
  ln -sf /opt/uvr/bin/uvr /usr/local/bin/uvr
  ln -sf /opt/quarto/bin/quarto /usr/local/bin/quarto
  ln -sf /opt/arf/bin/arf /usr/local/bin/arf
  cat >> "$SINGULARITY_ENVIRONMENT" <<'EOF'
unset R_HOME
export LANG=C.UTF-8
export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
export SPACK_VIEW=/opt/views/view
export PATH="/usr/local/bin:/opt/views/view/bin:${PATH}"
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="/opt/views/view/lib/pkgconfig:/opt/views/view/lib64/pkgconfig:/opt/views/view/share/pkgconfig:${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:-}"
export CPATH="/opt/views/view/include:${CPATH:-}"
export LIBRARY_PATH="/opt/views/view/lib:/opt/views/view/lib64:${LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="/opt/views/view/lib:/opt/views/view/lib64:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
EOF
%test
  set -eu
  command -v R
  command -v Rscript
  command -v uvr
  command -v quarto
  command -v arf
  R --version
  uvr --version
  quarto --version | grep -Fx "1.9.38"
  arf --version | grep -Fx "arf 0.5.2"
  LANG=C.UTF-8 LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 Rscript --vanilla -e 'quit(status = if (l10n_info()[["UTF-8"]]) 0 else 1)'
  test -r /opt/views/view/lib/libopenblas.so.0
  # The project R library is not present during image construction.
  Rscript --vanilla -e 'stopifnot(capabilities("cairo"))'
  command -v gfortran
  command -v pkg-config
  gdal-config --version
  geos-config --version
  pkg-config --exists gdal geos proj sqlite3 absl_base
  pkg-config --exists cairo freetype2 libpng libtiff-4 libjpeg libwebp libwebpmux
  test -r "$(fc-match --format '%{file}' sans)"
  test -r /opt/views/view/lib/libudunits2.so.0 || test -r /opt/views/view/lib64/libudunits2.so.0
  test -r /opt/views/view/share/udunits/udunits2.xml
  test -r /opt/views/view/share/proj/proj.db
  r_home=$(R RHOME)
  test -r "${r_home}/lib/libR.so"
  test -r /opt/spack-environment/spack.lock
  test ! -e /opt/spack/bin/spack
{% endblock %}

title: 13  Lock and Synchronize R Packages
text:
uvr.toml declares direct R requirements and uvr.lock records their resolved versions. The SIF supplies the stable R ABI and the uvr executable. At runtime, uvr owns its project library, cache, R-version resolution, and activation files; the container and runner do not override them.
The direct declaration covers the implemented pipeline and the reviewed stage 5–7 spatial workflow. The following survey parsed all ten top-level legacy R scripts at commit 31e0769683e133e136b09ac0c6608c5a12657a9a, including namespaced calls and 999_utility_functions.R. Comments and checkpoint copies are not executable dependencies.







Legacy evidence
Required packages and migration treatment




Stages 0–7: tidyverse, magrittr, CSV/Excel readers
Declare the used members dplyr, ggplot2, purrr, readr, stringr, tibble, tidyr, plus magrittr and readxl; avoid requiring the entire tidyverse bundle


Stages 0, 2–4A: data.table, rlang, stringi
Retain as explicit requirements, including legacy replication fixtures


Stage 0 imports openxlsx; page 18 still imports it
Declare openxlsx even though the legacy script does not call its readers


Stages 5–7: sf
Geometry I/O, validity repair, unions, relations, areas, CRS, containment, and centroids


Stage 5: igraph
graph_from_adjacency_matrix() and components() for contiguity diagnostics


Shared utility: fuzzyjoin; stage 6: stringdist
Grouped cosine string-distance joins and clinic-name matching; declare both explicitly


Stage 5: tmap, ggpubr, MetBrewer, ggplot2
Reviewed map diagnostics, plot assembly/export, and palettes; retained for the planned plot-list targets


Stage 3: gtranslate
Replaced by the recorded translation artifact in S3; do not introduce live translation into targets


Stages 4A, 5, 7: feather
Migrated tabular artifacts use DuckDB/Parquet; sf targets retain geometry. No standalone feather or Arrow C++ runtime is required


Stage 4A: furrr, parallel
targets owns execution; no nested futures. parallel is supplied with R


Every main script: rstudioapi
IDE working-directory setup is replaced by the runner and project paths


data_checks.R: diffdf
Legacy scratch comparison only; maintained checks use explicit schema/value comparisons


Commented ggsflabel calls
Excluded; no active reference in the reviewed scripts



The lock resolves transitive packages such as stars, tmaptools, and raster dependencies of mapping packages; they are not all promoted to direct requirements. units and s2 are direct requirements because the runtime acceptance check exercises them explicitly. Native dependencies belong in Spack, not in this package list. The pinned legacy mapping calls use tmap v3 syntax; migrating those diagnostics to the resolved tmap API and checking their meaning is stage-5 implementation work, not a reason to pin an untested old mapping stack here.
